newsitem.title: INDIA: India launches rescue effort after killer cyclone.
newsitem.headline: India launches rescue effort after killer cyclone.

text.p: Indian authorities scrambled to launch rescue operations on Friday after as many as 1,000 people were feared killed by a cyclone that lashed the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.

Communications and transport routes to the worst affected areas were severely disrupted. Torrents of water have swept away bridges while winds threw trees across highways and blew down telephone lines, officials said.

Police and troops on Friday battled swirling waters between two and three metres (seven and 10 feet) deep to reach many coastal villages. Military helicopters dropped food packages and drinking water to the stranded, officials said.
"The momentum of the relief operation is building up now," said R.V. Chandravadan, a magistrate in Rajahmundry town, at the heart of the devastation.
The state's Chief Minister V. Chandrababu Naidu told reporters after making an aerial survey of the area the death toll could climb as high as 1,000.
"The rice bowl of the state looks like a burial ground," Naidu said late on Thursday.
Police in the capital Hyderabad put the death toll at more than 500 and officials said the cyclone destroyed houses, livestock and crops. Troops were mobilised to help relief work.
State government spokesman Nageswara Rao put the number of homes destroyed or damaged in the deluge at 400,000 and said several thousand people had been injured.
The United News of India agency said seven people had been admitted to hospital with symptoms similar to cholera, as health workers faced a possible epidemic.
The seven were staying at a relief camp near the port of Kakinada, where the cyclone, with winds gusting up to 180 kph (110 mph), made landfall late on Wednesday.
Tidal waves swept up to five km (three miles) inland, submerging many towns and villages when the cyclone struck. It raged for five hours before moving inland and losing power.
Around 3.5 million people live in the fertile Konaseema region around the Godavari river delta south of Kakinada, which took the brunt of the storm.
Around two million people had been affected by the disaster, Rao said. He said the ministry had not assessed an exact death toll "because of the inaccessibility of places".

About 100 soldiers and eight doctors had fanned out in the East Godavari district to begin relief operations, Chandravadan said. Six helicopters were flying continuous trips to drop supplies to stranded villagers, he said.
Most people were killed by flooding, house collapse or electrocution as gale force winds and heavy rains wrecked their mud and thatch homes, officials said.
Authorities said 70 fishermen were also missing.
Naidu put a provisional estimate on losses in the East Godavari district, hit hardest by the cyclone, at 20 billion rupees ($560 million).

H.S. Brahma, the official coordinating relief in Hyderabad, 200 miles (320 km) to the west of Kakinada, said more than 100,000 people were being sheltered in 400 relief camps set up in East and West Godavari districts.
Weather officials said the cyclone had fizzled out.
Reddy Subramaniam, a tax collector in Rajahmundry, said 2,500 livestock had been lost, and 250,000 hectares (625,000 acres) of rice paddy inundated.

Andhra Pradesh's flat coastline renders it vulnerable to tropical storms tearing in off the Bay of Bengal. In 1977, more than 10,000 people were killed by a cyclone that drove a tidal wave up to 12 km (eight miles) inland.
A cyclone killed 120 people in June this year, and 967 people died in 1990.
